references.text: The Ten Commandments forbid the worship of other gods and describe the Lord as a jealous God (אֵל קַנָּא), the same expression used in Exodus 34:14.
The repetition of the Ten Commandments in Deuteronomy also describes the Lord as a jealous God (אֵל קַנָּא).
Moses warns Israel against following other gods and reminds them that the Lord is a jealous God (אֵל קַנָּא) among them.
The Lord is described as a consuming fire and a jealous God (אֵל קַנָּא).
Joshua describes the Lord as a holy and jealous God (אֵל־קַנּוֹא) who will not forgive apostasy.
Nahum begins by declaring that the Lord is a jealous and avenging God (אֵל קַנּוֹא).
Earlier in Exodus, worship of other gods is forbidden, with the command to tear down their sacred pillars.
The Lord declares that he will not give his glory to other gods or his praise to idols.
Paul warns against provoking the Lord's jealousy (παραζηλοῦμεν τὸν κύριον) by participating in idol worship.
Jesus quotes the command to worship the Lord alone when he rejects Satan's temptation (κύριον τὸν θεόν σου προσκυνήσεις).
A direct theological parallel between the two legal codes confirming God's jealous nature as the basis for the prohibition against idolatry.
